title: A wave, a coupon and a computer-generated spokesman
lede: The launch reached almost everyone. What Coca-Cola could not buy was permission to take the old drink away. We have no figure for what the campaigns cost, and we do not guess.

blocks.title: Seven weeks in: who knew, and who had tried it
blocks.subtitle: Americans aware of the change by June 1985, in millions, as estimated by the president of Coca-Cola USA.

to.label: Had tried the new Coke
to.note: “About 80 percent said they would repurchase,” Dyson said.[^5]

to.label: Aware, had not tried it (derived remainder)

blocks.source: Brian Dyson, quoted by UPI, Jun 10, 1985.[^5] These are the company’s own estimates. The remainder is derived.

blocks.title: Two campaigns for two Cokes
blocks.body:
After July 1985 the company advertised both. Its own history describes “the youthful, leading-edge ‘Catch the Wave’ campaign for the new taste of Coke and the emotional ‘Red, White and You’ for Coca-Cola classic.”[^1]

In May the newspaper advertisements had said of those who tried the new taste: “Seventy percent of them can’t wait to get more.”[^4]

blocks.title: The coupon
blocks.body:
Callers to the hotline were offered a coupon for a free six- or eight-pack of the new Coke. Dyson said 90% of callers accepted, and read that as willingness to try the product.[^4][^5]

One caller told UPI he had phoned to complain, waited ten minutes on hold and was promised a coupon for the drink he was complaining about.[^4]

blocks.title: The 2019 campaign
blocks.body: Thirty-four years later the failure was the selling point. Coca-Cola said Netflix executives visited its archives in Atlanta to study the 1985 packaging and advertising, and that the Duffer Brothers directed an advertisement that put the show’s cast into a 1980s Coca-Cola spot.[^25] A Coca-Cola director, Peter Shoemaker, was quoted as saying that recreating the product “took about six months and was top secret.”[^26]
